pairs.rationale: Both identify Joseph through Davidic ancestry. Luke makes his belonging to David's house the reason for the Bethlehem journey; Matthew's angel addresses him as Joseph, son of David, without narrating this census journey.

Both describe Mary as betrothed to Joseph and pregnant. Matthew additionally attributes conception to the Holy Spirit and says it occurred before they came together; Luke's cited registration notice does not repeat those explanations.

Both infancy accounts describe the time to give birth arriving. Luke1 concerns Elizabeth and immediately reports her son's birth; Luke2 concerns Mary in Bethlehem and narrates the birth next. This is a repeated birth-transition pattern, not the same mother or event.

The later angelic sign repeats the infant's swaddling cloths and manger from the narrated birth. This connects the sign with the precise circumstances already given, without supplying independent testimony to the lodging-place detail.

Both infancy scenes describe an angel appearing and the recipients becoming afraid. Luke2 adds the Lord's surrounding glory and concerns shepherds in the fields; Luke1 concerns Zechariah at the incense altar. The places and recipients remain distinct.

Both angelic announcements begin with reassurance against fear and associate a child's birth with joy. Luke2 promises good news of great joy for the people; Luke1 addresses Zechariah about John and many rejoicing at his birth.

Both angelic announcements connect the Child's birth with salvation. Luke calls the newborn Savior, Christ and Lord in David's city; Matthew commands the name Jesus because He will save His people from sins. The additional titles and future-versus-born announcement remain distinct.
The angel's sign specifically matches the swaddled infant lying in the manger in the earlier birth notice. It identifies the narrative's sign rather than creating an independent account.

Luke describes the heavenly army praising God, while the psalm calls all God's angels and powers to praise Him. The shared heavenly praise is explicit; the psalm's powers wording is not rewritten as a second narrative of this angelic appearance.

Both Lukan acclamations join glory in the highest with peace. Here the heavenly praise names peace on earth among people of God's favor; the entry acclamation names peace in heaven. The speakers, occasions and placement of peace remain distinct.
The shepherds find the infant lying in the manger, matching the angel's announced sign. Mary and Joseph are added in the discovery; the earlier sign also specifies swaddling cloths.

Both scenes describe witnesses reporting revealed news concerning Jesus after an angelic encounter in the surrounding account. Here shepherds report the birth saying after seeing the Child; later women report the tomb news to the Eleven and others. This compares different birth and resurrection testimony scenes.

Both notices describe Mary keeping all these matters in her heart. Luke2:19 adds pondering after the shepherds' news; the later notice follows the twelve-year-old Jesus' temple episode. The repeated maternal response is not the same occasion.

Both scenes conclude an encounter concerning Jesus with return and praise of God. The shepherds return praising for what they heard and saw; the later disciples return to Jerusalem with joy and bless God in the temple. The groups, places and events differ.
The circumcision on the eighth day follows the law's eighth-day circumcision instruction. Leviticus does not supply Jesus' naming or the angelic naming promise.

Jesus' name at circumcision matches the angel's earlier command that Mary name her promised Son Jesus. The earlier announcement precedes conception in its narrative context, as the naming notice recalls.

Luke connects completed purification days with Moses' law and presentation in Jerusalem. Leviticus specifies the mother's purification offering at the Tent of Testimony. Luke's plural their and the Child's presentation are retained; Leviticus is not made to require purification of everyone included in that plural.

Luke's law citation about the womb-opening firstborn being holy to the Lord corresponds to the command to consecrate every firstborn opening the womb as belonging to God. Exodus includes animals as well as humans; Luke's citation specifies every male.

Both specify two turtledoves or two young pigeons as the offering. Leviticus explains this provision when the person's resources cannot supply a lamb and distinguishes the two sacrifices; Luke quotes the permitted birds without reproducing the full rule.

Simeon's expectation of Israel's consolation corresponds to Isaiah's command to comfort God's people and Jerusalem. Isaiah is a restoration promise, not an independent biographical notice about Simeon or his Spirit-endowment.

Both promises postpone death until a specified sight of God's messianic work. Simeon is promised sight of the Lord's Christ; Jesus later tells some followers they will see God's kingdom before tasting death. The recipients and promised sights are not equated, and no common fulfillment date is assigned.

The parents' arrival with Jesus for the law's custom continues the earlier notice of bringing Him to Jerusalem for presentation. This identifies the narrated visit that intersects Simeon's Spirit-led arrival; it is not an independent witness to the visit or to the Spirit's guidance.

Both speakers connect death or release with seeing the awaited person. Israel says he may die after seeing Joseph alive; Simeon acknowledges being released in peace according to God's word, after seeing salvation as the surrounding hymn states. The persons and circumstances remain distinct; Luke does not state Simeon's age.

Simeon's eyes seeing God's salvation correspond to Isaiah's promise that earth's ends will see salvation from God. Luke gives one person's present testimony about the Child, while Isaiah announces a public, worldwide revelation.

Both place God's salvation before the nations or peoples. Luke describes salvation prepared in all peoples' sight; Isaiah describes the Lord uncovering His holy arm before all nations and the earth's ends seeing salvation.

Both combine Israel's restoration with light and salvation for nations. Isaiah names Jacob's tribes and Israel's dispersion before the servant's light for nations; Luke names revelation to nations and glory for Israel, preserving the different formulations.

Both passages associate God's intervention with contrasting outcomes in Israel and the fall of many. This supplied Isaiah text contrasts a sanctuary for trust with Jacob's trap and people's falling; Simeon speaks of the Child's appointment for falling and rising. Isaiah's conditional wording is retained rather than replaced by another edition's stone wording.

Both join a penetrating sword image with the soul and disclosure or judgment of heart-thoughts. Luke's statement concerns Mary's own soul and the revelation of many hearts; Hebrews concerns God's living word. The comparison does not identify Mary's sword with the word or claim identical experiences.

Both associate widowhood with petitions and prayer night and day. Luke describes Anna's temple service and fasting; Timothy describes a widow left alone who hopes in God. Their settings and social descriptions are not treated as the same community status.

Both connect Jesus with hope for Israel's redemption. Anna speaks about the Child to those awaiting Jerusalem's redemption; the later travelers describe having hoped Jesus would redeem Israel after the passion. The different moments and degrees of understanding are preserved.

Both infancy accounts place the family in Galilee at Nazareth. Luke describes return after completing the Lord's law; Matthew narrates withdrawal after the Egyptian stay and fear of Archelaus. No single merged journey or chronology is imposed.

Both childhood summaries say the child grew and became strong. Jesus' summary adds wisdom and God's grace; John's adds strength in spirit and wilderness residence until his public appearance. The children and developmental settings remain distinct.

The annual Passover-family journey fits the law's recurring pilgrimage festivals, including Unleavened Bread and appearing before the Lord. Exodus specifies male attendance and other festivals, without naming Jerusalem here or requiring Mary's attendance in particular; Luke reports both parents' actual custom.

Both place Jesus in the temple in a learning-and-teaching encounter. Luke describes the twelve-year-old among teachers, listening and asking questions; John describes the adult teaching during a feast and people questioning His knowledge of writings. The ages, roles and occasions are not identified.

Both describe amazement at Jesus' understanding or knowledge. Luke's hearers marvel at the child's understanding and answers; John's hearers question the adult's knowledge without formal study. John does not narrate the childhood episode.

Both connect Jesus' temple activity with His Father. Luke preserves the phrase what belongs to My Father; John explicitly names My Father's house during the cleansing. House is not silently substituted into Luke's supplied wording.

Both notices describe close followers failing to understand Jesus' saying. Here they are His parents after the temple response; later they are disciples after the passion prediction. The repeated incomprehension pattern does not make the sayings or hearers identical.

Jesus' remaining subject to His parents corresponds to the instruction that children obey their parents in the Lord. Ephesians gives a general command; Luke narrates Jesus' childhood conduct and additionally returns to Mary's keeping matters in her heart.

Both childhood summaries describe growth and favor with God or the Lord and with people. Luke adds wisdom and age; Samuel's summary names Samuel and continued growth. This compares the stated childhood pattern without equating the children.

deferred.reason: Augustus's decree registering the inhabited world was read. No separate supplied passage precisely establishes this particular decree; generic Caesar or tax vocabulary was not used to manufacture a counterpart.

The first-registration notice naming Quirinius and Syria was read. Other registration notices do not establish this event's identity or resolve its chronology, so no historical identification or alternate timetable was invented.
Everyone's traveling to register in their own city was read. General census or travel passages were not treated as a precise counterpart to this particular registration procedure.
The shepherds' field residence and nighttime flock watches were read. Generic shepherd or night-watch passages were not counted as independently attesting this setting.

The shepherds' decision to go to Bethlehem after the angels departed was read. Repeating the immediately preceding announcement alone would not establish a sufficiently separate counterpart to this distinctive travel decision.
The hearers' wonder at the shepherds' report was read. Generic marveling in other infancy or miracle stories was not treated as a sufficiently precise counterpart to this response.

Simeon's receiving the Child into his arms and blessing God was read. Other child-blessing episodes differ in recipient and action, and no close independent counterpart was retained for this introduction to his hymn.
The parents' wondering at Simeon's words was read. Other reactions of amazement do not independently reproduce this parental response to these particular words.
Anna's named father, tribe, age and seven-year marriage history were read. Generic accounts of aged or devout widows do not establish these personal identities or biographical details.
Jesus' age of twelve at the customary festival journey was read. No supplied independent passage precisely attests this age and journey; no later educational custom or age rule was imported.

Jesus' remaining in Jerusalem without His parents' knowledge as they returned was read. Other children remaining at places of worship do not reproduce this unintended separation or the parents' lack of knowledge.

The parents' supposition about the traveling company and their search among relatives and acquaintances were read. No sufficiently precise independent counterpart was established for those circumstances.
The unsuccessful search and return to Jerusalem were read. General search or return narratives were not counted as precise evidence for this particular parental journey.
The parents' distress and Mary's question about the anguish of searching were read. Unrelated maternal suffering or surprise was not treated as reproducing this exchange.

review_notes: All 52 actual Luke 2 source units and every retained target passage were read from the exact Saints cached snapshots with relevant context. Original source words, identities, display text and continuation paragraphs are unchanged.

The supplied registration notices are retained without inventing a Quirinius chronology or equating unspecified censuses. Luke's Nazareth return and Matthew's Egyptian/Judean journey are compared without a merged infancy timetable.

Internal links identify precise sign/event correspondences, the repeated maternal heart-keeping formula, the parents' presentation visit and recurring infancy or response patterns. They are explicitly not independent historical attestation.

Luke's firstborn/presentation/circumcision and bird-offering references are compared with the actual Exodus and Leviticus wording. The plural their purification is not silently changed to her, and the laws are not made to require every action of every person in Luke's scene.
Isaiah's actual Greek-based sanctuary/trap wording in 8:14–15 is preserved. Salvation/light comparisons distinguish Simeon's present child testimony from Isaiah's wider restoration promises.
The sword/soul/heart-thoughts comparison with Hebrews is restricted to imagery and does not identify Mary's sword with God's word. Anna is not assigned another widow's identity or community office.

Father's house is not silently substituted for Luke2:49's what belongs to My Father. The temple-wisdom comparisons preserve child/adult ages, listening/questioning versus teaching, and distinct occasions.
Fourteen source units remain explicitly deferred with zero completion credit. Multiple targets for circumcision/naming earn only one distinct-source completion for Luke2:21.
